﻿BUSINESS PACKAGE | CANADIAN INDUSTRY | OCTOBER 2026
Eavor Technologies Inc.
Mark Fitzgerald, President & CEO · Matt Toews, Co-founder, CT&OO · Calgary, Alberta
What a drilled kilometre returns, and what Loop 2 has to prove before the design is sold as repeatable. Worked from Eavor's own May 2026 technical update, so every number below can be checked against your own page.
Prepared for: Eavor Technologies Inc. · Prepared by: Michael Crumly, Regina, Saskatchewan · Basis: public sources, cited throughout · Tone: operator to operator, no flattery, no ask.
Executive summary
Your update makes four claims that matter: the physics matched the pre-drill prediction, Loop 1 is under-built rather than under-performing, the cementing failure was the project-impacting event, and depth is the lever that takes output from about 2 MWe per loop to about 20 MWe. This package takes those claims at face value and does arithmetic on them.
The arithmetic leaves four open items that only Eavor can close: (1) the shape of the thermal decline after year 5, (2) the cost of a working lateral pair rather than a drilled one, (3) electricity conversion until the ORC plant is loaded, and (4) what must be demonstrated below 9 km TVD before capital commits to 15 km. Sections 1 to 4 take them in that order.
One framing note up front. Trade press compares roughly 0.5 MW delivered with the 8.2 MWe Phase 1 nameplate, about 6%. Your update shows why that is not like for like: one loop of four, four working lateral pairs of twelve, and an ORC plant sized for the whole project. This package does not use the 6% comparison. It uses your numbers.
Section 1: The conduction-tax math, from your own published figures
A sealed loop moves heat by conduction only. Your update says so directly: heat transfer to the wellbores is proportional to the area available for heat transfer, which gives the 4/12 = 33% expectation for four working pairs. Everything else follows from that.

	Read plainly: your own numbers say a working pair gives up roughly a third or more of its thermal output between early life and year 5. If that decline were smooth and exponential it is about 9% per year (1.3 / 2.1 ≈ 0.61 over five years). That is the conduction tax in one line, stated by Eavor.
The open question is what happens after year 5. If the same 9% per year persisted, a pair would be near 0.8 MWth at year 10, about 62% of the year-5 level. If the decline flattens as the heat-affected volume grows, it is higher. This is an illustration of why the shape matters, not a forecast. The curve beyond year 5 is not in the update, and it sets the 30 to 100 year economics the update describes.
Two numbers from the update that do not obviously reconcile and are worth one sentence from Eavor: average thermal duty since startup is given as 11.8 MWth, while current Loop 1 production is given as about 8.5 MWth. That is 28% lower now than the average. Is the difference early-transient decline, a change in the number of flowing pairs after flushing, or a different measurement basis?
Electricity. The update gives about 4.3% conversion at the 11.8 MWth average duty, with the ORC plant far below its design point. 11.8 × 0.043 ≈ 0.51 MW, which matches the roughly 0.5 MW in trade reports. Design point is about three quarters of project thermal, about 48 MWth. If 8.2 MWe is delivered at that point, the implied design conversion is about 17%. So the same ORC plant is the difference between about 4% and about 17%. Current thermal duty is about 25% of that design point (11.8 / 48).
Section 2: Where the learning curve actually bends
Your update names the execution variables. This table lines them up against Loop 1 so each one becomes a number that can be reported for Loop 2.

	Three variables bend the curve, in this order of leverage: cementing integrity (it decides whether parallel drilling is possible at all), lateral-pair completion rate (it sets output directly), and recovery of compromised laterals (it is the insurance on the first two). Your update says the fix is well-understood cementing design applied to this multi-lateral architecture, not new technology. The package takes that as the hypothesis Loop 2 tests.
The three-week-per-pair target gives a schedule check: 12 pairs at three weeks each is 36 weeks of drilling per loop if pairs are completed one after another, which is the figure to compare against Loop 1's actual calendar.
Section 3: The depth wall
Your update states that output rises steeply with depth: at a 30 °C/km gradient, a loop at 15 km produces about 20 MWe against about 2 MWe at Geretsried. It also states that below about 9 km TVD current drilling technology faces a limit, and that a purpose-built drilling system is being constructed, with a working system in the field in a few years. The first Geretsried loop reached about 8 km measured depth.
Taken together, the economic case for "geothermal anywhere" below $75/MWh depends on a tool that does not yet exist in the field. What has to be true, and the gates before capital commits:
Gate
	What must be shown
	1. Tool qualification
	The new drilling system drills beyond 9 km TVD on a real well, with bit life, rate of penetration and trip count reported against Geretsried's.
	2. Predict, then publish
	Before spud, file the predicted MWth per pair and cost per pair at depth. After flow testing, publish the measured value. Your update credits exactly this method on Loop 1 (the thermal output was predicted before any capital was spent). Apply it at depth.
	3. Cost per working pair at depth
	Cost and weeks per completed pair against the three-week benchmark. Depth buys output only if the pair cost does not rise faster.
	4. Heat engine fit
	Size the surface plant to the loops actually delivered. The ORC result above shows what an oversized plant does to conversion.
	Your update frames depth as a continuum with incremental loops. That is the right frame for risk: each loop buys one gate, and none of them needs the 15 km system to be proved first.
Section 4: What Loop 2 must prove, in numbers
A sequencing proposal. The thresholds are proposals for Eavor to replace with its own; the metrics are the ones your update already uses.

	Report it; a gate near 10 of 12 (83%) makes the loop an honest unit of the 64 MWth design
	2
	Share of pairs drilled with two rigs in parallel
	1 of 6
	All pairs in parallel, with no inter-rig hydraulic communication logged
	3
	Weeks per completed pair
	about double the plan
	At or near three weeks, reported per pair, not as an average
	4
	MWth per operating pair, early life
	about 2.1
	Within the pre-drill prediction, published
	5
	MWth per pair at year 5, and the curve to year 10
	1.3 at year 5 (stated); beyond year 5 not published
	A decline curve with a stated asymptote or a stated reason it has none
	6
	ORC load fraction and conversion
	about 25% of design point, about 4.3%
	Electricity reported against load fraction, so conversion is not read as a loop result
	The sequencing logic: gates 1 to 3 prove the loop can be built to plan. Gates 4 and 5 prove the heat is there at the cost modelled. Gate 6 stops the heat engine from masking either one. A licensee reading the Loop 2 report should be able to compute their own year-5 thermal from pair count alone.
Questions only Eavor can answer
* What is the decline curve for a working pair beyond year 5, and does it have an asymptote?
* Why is average thermal duty since startup (11.8 MWth) higher than current production (about 8.5 MWth)?
* What did a completed lateral pair cost at Geretsried, and what does the model assume for pair 12 of a Loop 2?
* Is the 2 MWe per loop at Geretsried depth a design-point figure at full ORC load?
Canadian-owned status
Eavor is headquartered in Calgary and led by Mark Fitzgerald. Foreign stakes are minority: OMV holds 6.5%, and Chubu holds 40% of the German project company, with Eavor holding 60%. No acquisition or change of control was found as of October 20, 2026.
What I can do next
I can turn Sections 1 and 4 into a one-page heat-per-pair ledger built against your measured Loop 2 numbers, and review the decline-curve model before it is published. If useful, tell me which. I do not know your constraints from the outside.
—Mike
Logic has to be an option.
michael@digamoni.ca — logical reply guaranteed.
